--- gd-head-tags: - >- ``{=html} open-graph: title: >- [Graph.densest_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Find the densest subgraph: the set of nodes with the most edges per node. twitter-card: title: >- [Graph.densest_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} | EdgeCase description: >- Find the densest subgraph: the set of nodes with the most edges per node. title: >- [Graph.densest_subgraph()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 bread-crumbs: false toc-depth: 3 description-meta: >- Find the densest subgraph: the set of nodes with the most edges per node. page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find the densest subgraph: the set of nodes with the most edges per node. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L78097-L78227){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-function} ```pythonsignature Graph.densest_subgraph( method="exact", iterations=1, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Densest subgraph](../assets/graphs/densest-subgraph.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="A clique of four nodes A, B, C, D, every pair joined, with a chain D–E–F hanging off D. The densest subgraph is the clique, in the accent color: 6 edges on 4 nodes, density 6 / 4 = 1.5. The chain dilutes it, since the whole graph has 8 edges on 6 nodes, density 8 / 6 = 1.33. The card shows the nodes [A, B, C, D] and both densities." width="100%"} The density of a set of nodes $S$ here is the number of edges among them divided by their number, $|E(S)| / |S|$ (half the average degree inside $S$). The densest subgraph is the set with the highest such density. It highlights the tightest core of a network: tightly knit groups of friends, coordinated accounts or bots in social media, dense regions of protein interaction networks, or fraud rings in transaction graphs. Unlike a clique, it does not require every pair to be connected. Methods: - `"exact"` (default): an optimal set, computed with maximum flows. - `"greedy++"`: peel off the node of smallest degree repeatedly and keep the densest intermediate set. One iteration (the default) is Charikar's peeling, which finds at least half the optimal density; more iterations converge towards the optimum. Edge direction, self-loops and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [method]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["exact"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : `"exact"` (default) or `"greedy++"`. [iterations]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of peeling passes for `"greedy++"` (ignored by `"exact"`). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[float, list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The density and the node IDs of the subgraph, in ascending order. A graph without edges gives `(0.0, [])`. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `method=` is unknown or `iterations` is less than 1. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The exact method uses Goldberg's (1984) reduction: for a guess $g = p / q$, a network with arcs from a source to every node, from every node to a sink, and both ways along each edge has a minimum cut below $q m n$ exactly when some set has density above $g$, and the source side of that cut is such a set. Starting from $g = m / n$, each step replaces $g$ by the density of the set found (Dinkelbach's method), and stops when no denser set exists. All capacities are integers, so the result is exact. Each step is one maximum flow (Dinic's algorithm), and few steps are needed in practice. Greedy++ (Boob et al., 2020) repeats the peeling with node loads that accumulate across passes, as in NetworkX; its densities match NetworkX's. ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~k_core`) : The largest set where every node keeps at least `k` neighbors. [](`~maximum_clique`) : The largest set where every pair is connected. [](`~density`) : The share of possible edges present, for the whole graph. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A clique of four with a tail: the clique has 6 edges on 4 nodes, denser than the whole graph's 8 edges on 6: ::: {#9e4b509a .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph.from_edges( [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("A", "D"), ("B", "C"), ("B", "D"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "F")] ) density, nodes = graph.densest_subgraph() density, [graph.get_label_from_id(n) for n in nodes] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (1.5, ['A', 'B', 'C', 'D']) ``` ::: ::: ### An echo chamber In `polbooks()`, two books about US politics are linked when Amazon customers often bought both, and the `leaning` attribute records each book's slant. The densest part of the network is a block of 24 books, almost all liberal, with 114 links between them, 4.75 per book against 4.2 in the whole network: ::: {#f0afeb98 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from collections import Counter polbooks = ec.polbooks() density, core = polbooks.densest_subgraph() leaning = polbooks.get_node_attrs("leaning") density, len(core), Counter(leaning[n] for n in core) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (4.75, 24, Counter({'liberal': 22, 'neutral': 1, 'conservative': 1})) ``` ::: ::: One pass of greedy peeling is guaranteed at least half the best density. Here it stops at a looser group of 60 books from both sides, while a second pass finds the block: ::: {#2dfe489e .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} one = polbooks.densest_subgraph(method="greedy++") two = polbooks.densest_subgraph(method="greedy++", iterations=2) (round(one[0], 2), len(one[1])), (round(two[0], 2), len(two[1])) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ((4.65, 60), (4.75, 24)) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#8e925cef .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} polbooks.layout_forceatlas2(seed=1).plot( layout="pos", color_by="leaning", highlight=core ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
